records.title: Record-high sea temperatures across UK waters in the 2026 marine heatwave, from the Channel to Liverpool Bay
records.description: Cefas WaveNet buoys recorded sea temperatures between May and August 2026 that were 3 to 4.5 C above the seasonal average at four highlighted sites, with several sites reaching their highest readings since monitoring began in 2002 and 2004. Readings included 21.7 C in Poole Bay, 21.4 C at Hastings, 21.1 C south-west of the Isles of Scilly and 22.3 C in Liverpool Bay. Cefas notes that heatwaves of this kind can raise the risk of harmful algal blooms, disease and non-native species, and scientists report octopus and unusual sharks in the south-west.

location.name: UK shelf waters: Channel, Scilly, Liverpool Bay
location.detail: Coastal buoy sites around England and Wales: Poole Bay and Hastings (English Channel), south-west of the Isles of Scilly (Celtic Sea approaches), Liverpool Bay (Irish Sea) and east-coast sites in the North Sea.

records.layer_rationale: Sustained thermal anomaly in the surface ocean measured by a national buoy network.
secondary_drivers: Prolonged high pressure and land heatwave
Long-term warming of about 0.3 C per decade

notes.harm: Cefas lists potential ecological risks (algal blooms, disease, non-native species) and reports octopus and unusual sharks in the south-west, but documents no mortality (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The Cefas release describes possible risks to fisheries and tourism but records no closure or loss (ref 1).
notes.scale: Anomalies of 3 to 4.5 C appear at buoys from the Channel to Liverpool Bay and the east coast, a national coastline rather than one site (ref 1).
notes.duration: Hastings was unusually warm from February, April was unusually high and the highest readings came in July and August 2026 (refs 1, 2); earlier heatwaves in 2023 and 2025 are recorded in this feed.
notes.significance: Agency monitoring reports and a Met Office statement on a prolonged heatwave, but no formal notice or enforcement (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: WaveNet recorded 22.3 C in Liverpool Bay on 11 July 2026, about 5.3 C above average, and 21.7 C in Poole Bay on 9 July.

measures.name: Liverpool Bay peak sea temperature
measures.note: 11 July 2026, about 5.3 C above average but not a site record (ref 1).

measures.name: Late-May anomaly range
measures.note: Upper end of the 2.6 to 4.4 C range on 25-26 May 2026 (ref 2).

signals: Cefas names fisheries and tourism among sectors at risk from marine heatwaves (ref 1).

trend.note: Cefas cites 0.3 C per decade of warming over 40 years and about four more heatwave events a year (ref 2).

records.public_contact: Cefas general enquiries through the contact page on cefas.co.uk.
corrective_actions: Cefas is analysing the data with partners on what warm seas could mean for ecosystems, industries and coastal communities (ref 1).

records.title: Prolonged spring 2025 marine heatwave west of Ireland and around Britain, following the record June 2023 event
records.description: The Met Office reported record April and May sea surface temperatures since 1982, up to 4 C above normal west of Ireland and 1.5 to 2.5 C above normal around the UK, after a heatwave that began in early March and had lasted over two months. Researchers say the June 2023 heatwave west of Ireland peaked at about 4 to 5 C above average. Plymouth Marine Laboratory reported more tuna and octopus, with octopus taking bait from crab pots.

location.name: West of Ireland and Celtic Sea shelf
location.detail: Northwest European shelf: waters west and south of Ireland, the Celtic Sea, the western English Channel and the UK coast.

records.layer_rationale: Persistent surface-ocean temperature extreme on the northwest European shelf.
secondary_drivers: Persistent high pressure with weak winds

notes.harm: PML reported species shifts toward more tuna and octopus; the source documents no mortality and cites NOAA only generally about die-offs (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: PML said octopus were taking bait from crab pots, which affects the shellfish industry (ref 2).
notes.scale: Anomalies spread from west of Ireland to the Celtic Sea and the UK coastline, a regional sea (ref 1).
notes.duration: The 2025 event ran more than two months from early March (ref 1) and follows the June 2023 heatwave, which scientists place among the strongest on record (refs 4, 5), so the pattern recurs.
notes.significance: National met services and Cefas issued reports and statements, with no formal notice, closure or enforcement (refs 1, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Sea surface temperatures were up to 4 C above normal west of Ireland and 1.5 to 2.5 C above normal around the UK, record highs for April and May since 1982 (Met Office, 22 May 2025).

trend.note: Met Office cites about 0.3 C per decade of warming over 40 years; Maynooth authors note 2021-2023 held three of the top four years for marine heatwave activity in Irish waters (ref 5).

records.public_contact: Met Office and Cefas publish general enquiry channels on metoffice.gov.uk and cefas.co.uk.
corrective_actions: CEFAS, PML and NOC are monitoring effects on ecosystems and fisheries (ref 1).

records.title: Northeast Atlantic and adjacent seas warming and acidifying faster than the global average, Copernicus Ocean State Report 9 finds
records.description: The ninth Copernicus Ocean State Report, published September 2025, finds that the northeastern Atlantic and adjacent seas are warming and acidifying at rates above the global average. It reports surface pH falling 0.017 units per decade from 1985 to 2023 and sea level rising 3.7 mm a year from 1999 to 2024. Around one-third of the region experienced severe-to-extreme marine heatwaves in 2023, and the Bay of Biscay is named among 2024 extreme heatwave areas.

location.name: Northeast Atlantic and adjacent seas
location.detail: The report chapter covers the northeastern Atlantic and adjacent European seas; the Faroe Plateau, Iberian coast and Celtic-Biscay Shelf are named as warming slower than the semi-enclosed seas but faster than the global average.

records.layer_rationale: Basin-scale carbonate chemistry, temperature and sea-level change documented in a peer-reviewed ocean assessment.

notes.harm: The chapter says about 17 percent of cold-water corals and 50 percent of seagrass experienced extreme, long-lasting marine heatwaves in 2024, a potential rather than a measured loss (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: About 17 percent of shellfish farms on European coasts lay in seas with severe-to-extreme heatwaves in 2024, but no closure or loss is reported (ref 1).
notes.scale: The pH, temperature and sea-level trends are assessed for the whole northeastern Atlantic and adjacent seas, a basin-level region (ref 1).
notes.duration: The pH decline is measured over 1985 to 2023 and the warming trend over 1982 to 2024, so the change is multi-decadal (ref 1).
notes.significance: A scientific assessment report with no regulatory, treaty or court action attached (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Surface pH in the northeastern Atlantic is declining by 0.017 units per decade (1985 to 2023) while sea surface temperature rises 0.27 C per decade (1982 to 2024).

measures.name: Region waters with severe-to-extreme heatwaves in 2023
measures.note: Some lasting up to four months (ref 1).

signals: Aquaculture and coastal tourism are named as threatened sectors (ref 1).
About 200 million people live on European coasts (ref 1).

trend.note: Marine heatwave duration rose from 8 days per event (1993-2002) to 9 days (2015-2024) (ref 1).

records.public_contact: Copernicus Marine Service publishes a user-support channel on marine.copernicus.eu.
corrective_actions: The authors call for regional ocean indicators, locally tailored action and stronger science-policy transfer (ref 1).

sources.title: Ocean change in the northeastern Atlantic and adjacent seas: a multi-dimensional challenge for the environment, society, and economy (OSR9 chapter 1.2)

conflicts: The release (ref 2) says the northeastern Atlantic warms at about twice the global rate, while the chapter (ref 1) says above the global trend and describes the pH rate as comparable to the global trend even though its abstract says acidifying faster than average.
missing_fields: No oxygen or deoxygenation data in the chapter, so none is reported here.
The assessed area is wider than the Northeast Atlantic sea (it includes the North Sea and adjacent seas).

records.title: Toconao plastic pellet spill from lost containers reaches beaches in Galicia, Asturias and Cantabria; criminal case dismissed in 2026
records.description: The container ship Toconao lost six containers about 80 km off Viana do Castelo, Portugal on 8 December 2023, one holding about 26 tonnes of plastic pellets in 1,040 sacks. Pellets reached Galicia from 13 December and Galicia raised an alert to level 2 on 9 January 2024. In January 2026 a Noia court permanently closed the criminal case, finding no crime and no toxicity, while the Xunta says it spent over 2.3 million euros on cleanup.

location.name: Galician coast and Corrubedo lagoons
location.detail: Containers lost off northern Portugal; pellets stranded along Galicia, with plans also activated in Asturias and Cantabria. The court report names the Corrubedo and Carregal-Vixan lagoons and the Atlantic Islands National Park.

points.role: Corrubedo lagoons, named in the court ruling

records.layer_rationale: Loss of industrial plastic pellets from a ship washed up on coastlines.
secondary_drivers: Container loss at sea in heavy weather

notes.harm: The Noia court cited expert analysis finding no toxicity and no damage to the Corrubedo and Carregal-Vixan dunes or the Atlantic Islands park, so harm is potential, though pellets are persistent (refs 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: Fishers searched for floating sacks and volunteers and crews cleaned beaches, and the Xunta operation covered over 630 beaches in 66 municipalities (refs 5, 6).
notes.scale: Pellets stranded on the Galician coast and prompted emergency plans in Asturias and Cantabria, a national coastline in the Bay of Biscay and Atlantic approaches (ref 1).
notes.duration: Pellets arrived from 13 December 2023 and cleanup, a liability claim and the court case continued into 2026 (refs 1, 5).
notes.significance: Galicia and Asturias activated level 2 emergency alerts, prosecutors and the Noia court opened proceedings, and the court ruled in January 2026 (refs 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: About 26 tonnes of pellets in 1,040 sacks of 25 kg were lost; Galicia had collected about 2.3 tonnes of pellets and 4.2 tonnes of other plastics by 15 January 2024 (Cedre).

trend.note: SASEMAR surveys found no further containers or floating objects through 19 January 2024 (ref 1); the criminal case was closed in January 2026 (ref 2).

records.title: Sandymount Strand rated Poor for bathing after wastewater overflows in Dublin Bay, improving in 2025 as Dun Laoghaire Baths is rated Poor
records.description: The EPA classified Sandymount Strand in Dublin Bay as Poor in 2023 and 2024, with local authorities required to advise against bathing all season, citing wastewater overflows, dog fouling and misconnections. In 2025 it improved to Sufficient and the restriction was lifted, while Dun Laoghaire Baths was rated Poor on its first classification because of wastewater overflows. Ireland's largest treatment plant at Ringsend serves about 40 percent of national wastewater and was being upgraded.

location.detail: Dublin Bay on the Irish Sea coast; Sandymount Strand and Dun Laoghaire Baths in Co. Dublin, downstream of the Ringsend wastewater works.

points.role: Dun Laoghaire Baths, rated Poor in 2025

records.layer_rationale: Treated and untreated wastewater and storm overflows entering coastal bathing water.

notes.harm: The EPA rated the beach Poor, meaning bathing-water quality below the Sufficient standard with a health risk to swimmers, though no illness count is given (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Local authorities had to issue notices advising against bathing for the whole season in 2023 and 2024, and the 2025 whole-season ban was reported by Dublin People (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: The finding is confined to Sandymount Strand and the Dun Laoghaire Baths in Dublin Bay (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Poor ratings in 2023 and 2024, an improvement in 2025, and a new Poor rating for Dun Laoghaire Baths in 2025 show a recurring problem (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A formal EPA classification and statutory all-season bathing advisory apply (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

trend.note: Poor sites fell from five in 2023 to two in 2024 and one in 2025 nationally; Sandymount rose to Sufficient (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Sewage-linked E. coli reaches Devon beaches and Lyme Bay mussel farm as south-west overflow spills total 407,006 hours in 2025
records.description: Plymouth Marine Laboratory traced E. coli from rivers and sewage overflows into Plymouth Sound and Lyme Bay, finding spikes on dry as well as wet days. The Environment Agency recorded 46,164 spills totalling 407,006 hours across the south-west region in 2025. Two contamination events at a Lyme Bay mussel farm in 2019 were traced to overflows on the Exe and Dart and caused a downgrade of its shellfish classification.

notes.harm: On 8 July 2024 E. coli counts at Plymouth beaches were well above the level considered Sufficient for bathing water, on a dry day (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: A Lyme Bay mussel farm had its shellfish safety classification downgraded after two contamination events, costing the business thousands in revenue (ref 1).
notes.scale: The study and the legal claim span Plymouth Sound, Lyme Bay and coastal towns across Devon and Cornwall (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Bathing-water poor days were tracked across 2012 to 2025 and rose again over the last five years (ref 1).
notes.significance: The shellfish classification downgrade is a formal action, and a group nuisance claim has been filed, but no enforcement result is in these sources (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Scotland to apply tighter seabed limit for sea-lice drug emamectin benzoate at salmon farms after evidence of harm to crustaceans
records.description: SEPA survey work in 2017 found emamectin benzoate near fish farms had a negative effect on crustacean abundance and richness at seabed concentrations well below the original 763 ng/kg standard. A new standard, recalculated in March 2023 to 272 ng/kg dry weight, replaces it, and the Scottish Government said in June 2024 it intends to direct SEPA to apply it at existing farms after 48 months. The industry warns of fewer treatment options for sea lice.

location.name: Scottish marine salmon farm sites
location.detail: Scottish marine finfish farms regulated by SEPA, in sea lochs and coastal waters; the cited government documents do not name individual sites.

records.layer_rationale: Veterinary medicine discharged from salmon pens accumulates in marine sediment.
secondary_drivers: Persistence of the compound in sediment

notes.harm: SEPA analysis of 2017 samples showed emamectin benzoate had a negative effect on crustacean abundance and richness, proportional to seabed concentration (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The Scottish Government expects the standard to reduce the number of sea-lice treatments allowed per production cycle, and industry cites limited alternatives (ref 2).
notes.scale: The standard applies to all licensed Scottish marine finfish farms, a national coastline (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The issue dates from the 2016 review and 2017 SEPA interim restrictions and runs to a 48-month phase-in from 2024; the compound is persistent (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: UKTAG recommended a new environmental quality standard and Ministers intend a formal Direction to SEPA (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The recalculated environmental quality standard is 272 ng/kg sediment dry weight, replacing 763 ng/kg wet weight set in 1999; implementation is planned after 48 months.

measures.name: SEPA requested cut in use at existing sites in 2017

signals: The fish farm industry raised significant concerns about sea-lice treatment options and unclear socio-economic impacts (ref 2).

trend.note: The standard has been revised several times (23.5, 131, then 272 ng/kg) and is not yet applied at existing farms (ref 1).

records.public_contact: Scottish Government water environment team, waterenvironment@gov.scot is listed on the consultation page.
corrective_actions: Ministers intend to direct SEPA to apply the new standard in 48 months, and SEPA will confirm authorised volumes per site (ref 2).
SEPA already applies the new standard to new farms and discharge increases (ref 1).

records.title: Shoreline retreat south of Figueira da Foz and at Costa Nova-Vagueira on Portugal's west coast prompts sand nourishment and breakwater studies
records.description: Portugal's environment agency APA reports the 3.5 km coast between Cova-Gala and Lavos south of Figueira da Foz retreated 14 m on average in 2018 to 2021 (5.5 m a year), with 52 percent of the stretch in extreme erosion. Further north, the Costa Nova to Areao coast retreated about 140 m on average from 1958 to 2021, though recent years show stabilisation. APA has prepared a beach nourishment project at Figueira da Foz and studied a detached breakwater off Vagueira.

location.detail: Portuguese Atlantic coast between Aveiro and Figueira da Foz: Cova-Gala to Lavos, and Costa Nova to Areao including Vagueira.

records.layer_rationale: Coastal erosion driven by sediment deficit and storms, with sea-level adaptation planning.

notes.harm: APA documents a mean retreat of 14 m and a maximum of 42.5 m in 2018 to 2021 south of Figueira da Foz, with 97 percent of the stretch eroding (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The cited APA pages describe protective projects but no closure, evacuation or lost use (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: Two stretches of one national coastline are covered, with a national coastal plan (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.duration: Retreat is documented from 1958 to 2021 at Costa Nova-Areao and from 2010 to 2021 south of Figueira da Foz (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: APA published formal intervention projects and the national coastal plan PAL XXI (refs 1, 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Storm Kathleen brings coastal flood warnings and flooded properties to the north Wales coast and Ireland's Munster coast in April 2024
records.description: Storm Kathleen coincided with spring tides in early April 2024. The Welsh Government said 35 properties had flooded internally by 16 April across Conwy, Ceredigion and Torfaen, and Natural Resources Wales issued coastal flood warnings on 9 April for places including Kinmel Bay, Llanfairfechan and Prestatyn. Existing defences prevented flooding in many areas, and coastal flooding and wave overtopping occurred in Munster.

records.title: Storm Ciaran brings red wind warnings, evacuations and coastal flood warnings to Jersey, Brittany and the Channel coast in November 2023
records.description: Storm Ciaran struck the Channel on 1 and 2 November 2023. Jersey recorded gusts of 102 mph and moved 35 people to hotels, while the Environment Agency expected flooding in 54 areas, mostly on England's south coast, and warned of significant coastal flooding. Western Brittany recorded gusts up to 110 mph, and Hampshire and the Isle of Wight declared a major incident.

location.name: Jersey and the western English Channel
location.detail: Channel Islands, Brittany and the English Channel south coast; the sources describe wind damage in Jersey and coastal flood risk along the English south coast.

records.layer_rationale: Storm surge, waves and coastal flood risk during a Channel storm.

notes.harm: Three people were taken to hospital in Jersey after home damage, and waves crashed over the harbour arm at Folkestone (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: All flights from Jersey, Guernsey and Alderney were cancelled for 2 November and hundreds of southern schools closed (ref 2).
notes.scale: Impacts span the Channel Islands, Brittany and the south coast of England (ref 2).
notes.duration: The storm lasted 1 and 2 November 2023, days rather than weeks (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Jersey Met issued a red warning, and Hampshire and the Isle of Wight declared a major incident citing risk to life (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Police reported a top speed of 102 mph in Jersey, and the Environment Agency expected flooding in 54 areas, mostly on England's south coast.

measures.note: Police figure; the Met Office recorded 93 mph at Jersey Airport (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Plastic seabed litter off north-west Wales and north-west England found carrying invasive barnacles
records.description: Cefas examined 41 pieces of plastic seabed litter collected off England and Wales and found two non-native barnacle species and four species of unknown origin on items such as bleach bottles, plastic sheeting and buckets. The Australian barnacle Austrominius modestus was found at 27 m and 32 m depth off north-west Wales and north-west England. Cefas says this is the first study to confirm invasive species spreading via seabed litter in UK waters.

location.name: Seabed off NW Wales and NW England
location.detail: Sampling off the coasts of England and Wales; the barnacle finds were off north-west Wales and north-west England (Irish Sea side), though the source does not name the sea.

records.layer_rationale: Plastic litter on the seabed acting as a vector for non-native species.

notes.harm: Invasive species were found attached to plastic litter, a potential ecological risk, but Cefas does not detail damage caused by the species found (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or access disruption is described (ref 1).
notes.scale: Litter was sampled from several locations off England and Wales (ref 1).
notes.duration: A study with a further 150 pieces under analysis, so work continues beyond one survey (ref 1).
notes.significance: A single agency research announcement, without formal notice or enforcement (ref 1).

records.title: Bay of Biscay winter fishing closures to stop common dolphin bycatch continue into a fourth year
records.description: Common dolphins and other small cetaceans are caught in fishing gear in the Bay of Biscay at rates ICES says exceed the limit for a favourable conservation status every year since 2018. After a French Conseil d'Etat order in March 2023, annual winter closures for vessels over eight metres were applied from 2024, and on 4 September 2026 the European Commission proposed extending the closure into winter 2027. The French observatory PELAGIS found 2025 bycatch mortality significantly lower than estimated before the closures.

location.name: Bay of Biscay
location.detail: Atlantic waters of France and Spain, with fleets from Belgium, the Netherlands and Portugal; winter closure covers vessels over 8 m using high-risk gear.

records.layer_rationale: Incidental fishing mortality of a protected cetacean population.

notes.harm: The Conseil d'Etat found the maximum limit for favourable conservation status in the North-East Atlantic had been exceeded every year since 2018, citing ICES opinions (ref 1); EIA reports more than 110,000 common dolphins bycaught in the Bay since 1990 (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: About 300 EU vessels over 8 m are affected by each closure and compensation is paid from the EMFAF or state aid (ref 4); IFAW cites a 30 million euro compensation package for the 2024 closures (ref 3).
notes.scale: The closure involves France, Spain, Portugal, Belgium and the Netherlands and covers the Bay of Biscay as a regional sea (ref 4).
notes.duration: Winter closures have run since January 2024 (ref 3) and the Commission proposed a fourth year on 4 September 2026 (ref 4); bycatch strandings have occurred in unprecedented numbers since 2016 (ref 3).
notes.significance: The Conseil d'Etat ordered the government to close fishing areas within six months on 20 March 2023 (ref 1) and the Commission is acting through a delegated act under the CFP (ref 4).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Since 2024 the Biscay closures have been effective in reducing incidental catches of dolphins; PELAGIS found 2025 dolphin bycatch mortality significantly lower than estimated for 2017 to 2023 (European Commission, 4 September 2026).

records.title: ICES advises zero catch for cod, haddock, whiting and Irish Sea plaice across the Celtic Seas
records.description: ICES advice for 2026, issued on 27 June 2025, recommended zero catch for Celtic Sea cod, haddock, whiting and herring, the first zero-catch advice ever for haddock. Advice issued in June 2026 for 2027 again recommends zero cod in the Irish Sea, Western Channel and southern Celtic Seas, zero haddock in the southern Celtic Sea and Western Channel and, for the first time, zero Irish Sea plaice. ICES calls the situation in the Celtic Sea and Irish Sea 'particularly concerning'.

location.name: Celtic Seas and Irish Sea demersal stocks
location.detail: Celtic Sea, Irish Sea and Western Channel stocks shared by Ireland, the UK and France.

records.layer_rationale: Commercial fish stocks in the Celtic Seas ecoregion are below biomass limits and recruitment has fallen.

notes.harm: Oceana UK's reading of the 2027 assessment is that only 133 tonnes of adult cod remain in the Western Channel and southern Celtic Sea stock, a 99% decrease from 2012 (ref 3); ICES says the number of Celtic Seas stocks below Blim has been rising (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: ICES warned zero-catch advice will have 'serious consequences' for fishing communities (ref 2); the Irish Sea plaice limit for 2026 was 614 tonnes and the Irish Sea haddock advice for 2027 is down 69% (ref 3).
notes.scale: The advice spans the Celtic Sea, Irish Sea and Western Channel stocks within one ecoregion, with ICES overviewing 48 demersal stocks from the North Sea to Iberia (ref 1).
notes.duration: Zero-catch advice was issued in June 2025 for 2026 (ref 1) and again in June 2026 for 2027 (ref 3), so two consecutive advice years.
notes.significance: ICES advice is a formal scientific recommendation, not an enforcement order; a Cefas assessment found most UK 2026 limits were not set in line with advice (ref 3).

records.title: Celtic Seas pollack: zero-catch advice cut the handline fishery to bycatch only, and advice for 2027 is reduced
records.description: ICES advised zero catch of pollack in subareas 6 and 7 (Celtic Seas and English Channel) for 2024 and 2025. In response the UK and EU agreed that pollack could only be caught as bycatch in 2024, and the Marine Management Organisation set up support for the affected fishers. ICES advice issued on 30 June 2026 allows total removals of up to 3,216 tonnes in 2027 but shows a 41 percent probability that spawning biomass falls below Blim in 2028.

location.detail: ICES subareas 6 and 7: west of Scotland, Irish Sea, Celtic Sea and English Channel; the handline fishery is concentrated off Cornwall and south-west England.

notes.harm: ICES projects 14,057 tonnes of spawning biomass in 2028 under the 2027 advice, with a 41% probability of falling below Blim (ref 3); the 2024 advice sheet advised zero catch for 2025 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The government said pollack 'can only be caught as bycatch in 2024', which affected hand-and-pole line fishers on under-10 m vessels (ref 2).
notes.scale: The advice covers one stock, pol.27.67, though across ICES subareas 6 and 7 (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: ICES advised zero catch for both 2024 and 2025 (refs 1, 2), and a reduced advice of 3,216 t is now valid for 2027 (ref 3).
notes.significance: The zero total allowable catch was set in EU-UK negotiations on ICES advice and triggered the MMO compensation and Fisheries and Seafood Scheme support (ref 2).

records.title: Northeast Atlantic mackerel fished well above scientific advice by the coastal states
records.description: ICES advised a 77 percent cut in mackerel catches for 2026, yet its forecast of 2026 catches is about 398,000 tonnes, roughly 128 percent above that advice. Only the UK, Norway, the Faroe Islands and Iceland agreed a 299,010-tonne total for 2026, with the EU and Greenland outside the deal, and no internationally agreed TAC exists. ICES put spawning biomass at about 3.2 million tonnes, just above the critical limit of 3.07 million, and advised up to 352,938 tonnes for 2027.

location.name: Northeast Atlantic mackerel stock
location.detail: Widely distributed pelagic stock fished by coastal states including the UK, Norway, the Faroe Islands, Iceland and the EU;

records.layer_rationale: Shared stock whose catch limits are set unilaterally above advice because the coastal states have no sharing agreement.

notes.harm: ICES estimated 2026 spawning biomass at about 3.2 million tonnes, just above the 3.07 million tonne critical limit and below the 4.12 million tonne precautionary level, with a 33.2% probability of falling below the limit in 2028 (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: Mackerel, Atlanto-Scandian herring and blue whiting fisheries lost MSC certification more than five years ago and some European brands and retailers are switching to alternatives (ref 1).
notes.scale: The stock spans the Northeast Atlantic and several coastal states; the EU and Greenland sit outside the 2026 four-party arrangement (ref 3).
notes.duration: Total catch limits have exceeded scientific advice by 5% to 80% since 2009, and by 39% on average in 2020 to 2024 (ref 2).
notes.significance: ICES advice is formal but does not set national quotas, and the Marine Conservation Society downgraded midwater-trawled mackerel to rating 4 in April 2025 (refs 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Iceland capelin: zero-catch advice in 2024, a tiny quota in 2025 and a sharp fall in autumn 2026 advice
records.description: Iceland's Marine and Freshwater Research Institute advised zero capelin catch for winter 2024/25 after the autumn 2024 survey, then 8,589 tonnes in February 2025. Advice recovered to 197,474 tonnes for 2025/26, but after the September 2026 survey came in well below expectations the new advice for the coming season is 105,773 tonnes, about 70 percent below the 358,044 tonnes proposed in June 2026. The institute says incomplete survey coverage means the stock is probably underestimated.

location.name: Iceland-East Greenland-Jan Mayen capelin stock
location.detail: Capelin stock surveyed in the Iceland-East Greenland-Jan Mayen area, off east Greenland and north of Iceland.

records.layer_rationale: Fish stock whose recruitment and survey results swing from failure to recovery and back.

notes.harm: The autumn 2024 survey put spawning stock biomass at about 193,000 tonnes and found the harvest control rule's 95% probability of staying above Blim of 114,000 tonnes could not be met (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Zero catch was advised for winter 2024/25 and only 8,589 tonnes were advised in February 2025 (refs 1, 2), so almost no winter capelin catch was advised that season.
notes.scale: A single shared stock, the Iceland-East Greenland-Jan Mayen (IEGJM) capelin, is involved (ref 3).
notes.duration: Advice swung from zero (October 2024) to 8,589 t (February 2025), 197,474 t (January 2026) and 105,773 t (October 2026) across three seasons (refs 1 to 5).
notes.significance: The advice follows the harvest control rule agreed by the coastal states and was issued jointly with the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources (refs 1, 5).

key_measure.text: New capelin catch advice for the coming season is 105,773 tonnes, replacing the initial 358,044 tonnes; the fishable stock is just under 560,000 tonnes (MFRI, 12 October 2026).

records.title: Faroe Islands pilot whale and dolphin drive hunts killed more than 1,000 animals in 2025
records.description: Sea Shepherd counted 992 cetaceans killed across ten hunts in 2025 by 13 September, and Geographical reports more than 1,000 pilot whales and white-sided dolphins for the year, while the official count of the 13 September Fuglafjordur hunt was 285 pilot whales, excluding juveniles and foetuses. A further hunt near Sandavagur in early May 2026 killed more than 125 animals in the official toll, which excludes at least 15 foetuses and small juveniles. The hunt has no fixed quota and the UK-Faroe trade arrangements are due for review at the end of 2026.

notes.scale: Hunts occur at bays across the Faroese islands, a national-waters scale; the sources report about 900 animals a year since 2010 (ref 2).
notes.duration: The article reports an average of about 900 pilot whales and dolphins killed a year since 2010 and a tradition dating to around 800 CE (ref 2); EIA reports a 2010 to 2020 average of 685 pilot whales and 114 dolphins a year (ref 3).
notes.significance: A UK Early Day Motion backed by 72 MPs condemns the hunt and the Faroe trade arrangements are scheduled for review at the end of 2026 (ref 2).

records.title: Iceland fin whaling resumes in 2026 under a licence to 2029 as a bill to ban whaling is planned
records.description: Iceland granted Hvalur hf. a five-year licence in December 2024 to take up to 209 fin whales a year in 2025 to 2029, and its minke licence-holder 217 minke whales. Hvalur did not hunt in 2025 because Japanese meat prices were too low, but resumed in 2026, with 80 fin whales caught by 8 September against a quota of up to 150. The government says it will submit a bill in February 2027 that could permanently ban whaling.

notes.harm: Humane World for Animals counted 80 fin whales caught in Icelandic waters up to 8 September 2026, a species listed vulnerable by the IUCN (ref 4); the 2015 survey estimated about 44,000 fin whales (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or coastal livelihood loss is documented in the cited pages; Hvalur cancelled the 2025 season on weak Japanese meat prices (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The licence covers Icelandic national waters, with a quota of up to 150 fin whales in 2026 and 209 a year licensed to 2029 (refs 1, 4).
notes.duration: Hvalur resumed whaling in 2022 and the licence runs from 2025 to 2029 (refs 1, 4).
notes.significance: The government will submit a bill in February 2027 that could ban whaling, after a 2023 report found harpooned whales took two hours to die (ref 4); no ban is in force.

records.title: Scottish salmon farms record more than 35 million officially reported deaths from 2023 to 2025
records.description: Scottish farms officially reported 35,867,788 salmon deaths between January 2023 and October 2025, according to freedom of information data obtained by Animal Equality UK. The Animal and Plant Health Agency inspected 21 of 213 active sites in that period, with two unannounced inspections, and none of the 20 sites with the most deaths. A Scottish Parliament committee criticised the government's slow progress on regulating salmon farming in January 2025.

records.title: Galician shellfish beds collapse after low-salinity and heat events in the Rias Baixas
records.description: A December 2023 mass mortality reportedly killed about 95 percent of Galicia's cockles and 75 percent of Japanese clams after rainfall 127 percent above normal and salinity near 5 parts per thousand. Bivalve harvests in the Ria de Arousa fell from 2,700 tonnes in 2023 to 1,700 tonnes in 2024, and mussel production in 2024 was the lowest in 25 years. About 3,500 licensed shellfish gatherers remain, half as many as in 2001.

notes.harm: A December 2023 mass mortality reportedly killed about 95% of Galicia's cockles and 75% of Japanese clams (ref 1); cockle numbers fell about 80% in 2023 against 2022 (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: About 3,500 licensed mariscadoras remain, half as many as in 2001, and pickers on Illa de Arousa struggled to collect 1 kg of clams (ref 1).
notes.scale: The four Rias Baixas estuaries along Galicia's south-west coast are affected (ref 1).
notes.duration: Stocks had not recovered by June 2024 (ref 1), mussel production in 2024 was 178,000 t against 250,000 t in 2021 (ref 2), and Arousa harvests fell 2,700 t to 1,700 t from 2023 to 2024 (ref 3).
notes.significance: The sources are news and a monitoring-service use case; EcoWatch reports no formal government response in the cited coverage (ref 2).

records.title: Iberian orcas keep damaging and sinking sailing yachts off Portugal and Galicia
records.description: A small group of endangered Iberian orcas has been striking the rudders of sailing yachts since 2020. A yacht with five people aboard sank off Fonte da Telha near Lisbon in September 2025, and on 24 July 2026 another yacht sank near Estaca de Bares, Galicia, with its two occupants rescued. More than 500 interactions have been recorded and Spanish authorities advise sailors in orca zones to follow official guidance.

records.title: Wester Ross maerl beds recover after a ten-year scallop dredging ban, with threats remaining
records.description: Scallop dredging was banned in 2016 across the 600 square kilometre Wester Ross Marine Protected Area, the world's largest for maerl, and a decade of citizen-science surveys and local reports describe recovering scallops and fish and more sightings of whales, porpoises and dolphins. The surveys also found damaged maerl in some places from illegal dredgers and invasive algal growth that scientists suspect is linked to salmon-farm nutrients. In June 2026 Environmental Standards Scotland found that Scottish Ministers had failed their legal duties to protect and restore the seafloor.

records.layer_rationale: Protected maerl habitat that is slowly recovering from dredging damage.

notes.harm: BHA surveys highlighted damaged maerl in some locations from illegal dredgers and invasive algal growth, and a single pass of heavy towed gear can crush or bury up to 70% of maerl (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Creel fishing, hand diving and prawn trawling in designated areas remain allowed, and local creel and dive fishers report better catches since the ban (ref 1).
notes.scale: The protection applies to one 600 sq km marine protected area (ref 1).
notes.duration: The dredging ban dates from 2016 and BHA has surveyed the maerl for ten years (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: ESS found Scottish Ministers non-compliant with the Marine Strategy Regulations 2010 on seafloor monitoring (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: First UK-wide bycatch analysis finds thousands of seabirds, cetaceans and seals killed each year
records.description: A June 2026 analysis by the Wildlife and Countryside Link coalition estimates that UK fishing boats catch over 10,000 seabirds, over 1,000 cetaceans, around 500 seals and over 120 tonnes of protected sharks, skates and rays every year. It says the totals are likely the tip of the iceberg because only a fraction of the fleet is monitored. A two-year Cornish trial found towed deterrents cut the chance of seabirds being caught in gillnets by 59 to 71 percent.

location.name: UK waters, bycatch of protected species
location.detail: UK waters, spanning the North Sea and Atlantic seas; the gillnet deterrent trial involved Cornish fishing vessels.

records.layer_rationale: Incidental killing of protected species by fishing gear.

notes.harm: WCL's extrapolation is over 10,000 seabirds, over 1,000 cetaceans, around 500 seals and over 1,000 Atlantic salmon killed each year, plus six humpback and 30 minke whales found dead in Scottish creel ropes (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The report documents no fishery closure or loss of livelihood; it asks for remote electronic monitoring and mitigation, and trials in Filey Bay cut bycatch from 700 seabirds to four or five (ref 2).
notes.scale: The analysis spans UK waters across several seas and finds bycatch is a key reason the UK fails to reach good environmental status in some seas (ref 2).
notes.duration: The report says deaths have stayed 'stubbornly high' for decades despite known impacts (ref 1).
notes.significance: This is an NGO coalition analysis; Defra says it is acting through its Clean Catch programme and the Cornish trial results were published in Conservation Letters (refs 2, 3).

records.title: Repeated SHEFA-2 subsea cable faults off Orkney cut broadband to Shetland for 11 and 25 days in 2025
records.description: The SHEFA-2 fibre cable linking the Faroe Islands, Shetland, Orkney and mainland Scotland was damaged twice in 2025 off Orkney, in July (a fishing vessel is believed responsible) and October (cause not determined at the time). Shetland News reported outages of about 11 days and about 25 days for customers of providers without a backup route. The operator told a parliamentary inquiry that the cable has suffered over 20 major breaks since 2007, and the Scottish Government has since committed to the pre-development phase of a second cable.

records.title: Korean fish farms lose a record 143 billion won to heat in 2024 and face repeat die-offs in 2025 and 2026
records.description: Korea's National Institute of Fisheries Science put 2024 aquaculture losses from extended extreme sea temperatures at 143 billion won, the largest since records began, and farms in South Jeolla and South Gyeongsang reported millions of dead fish. High-temperature die-offs recurred in 2025 and again in summer 2026, when 360,707 farmed fish had been reported dead nationwide by early August, about five times the same point in 2025, and the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries raised its high-water-temperature alert to the top level. The ministry is distributing liquid oxygen systems, urging early harvest and moving some farms to cooler sites. Korean aquaculture losses from the 2024 heat reached a record 143 billion won, including 25.82 million fish and shellfish dead on South Jeolla farms alone. Heat advisories came earlier in 2025, and by 4 September 2026 a further 13.533 million farmed fish had died at 455 farms as the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries raised its high-temperature disaster alert. The Korea Meteorological Administration reports marine heatwave days around Korea at 83.3 a year over the past decade against 22.6 on the long-term average.

notes.scale: Die-offs were reported in several provinces from Jeju to the west coast, a national coastline rather than one bay (refs 1, 3, 5).
notes.duration: Losses are documented for 2024, 2025 and 2026; water at 28 C or above lasted 71 days from 24 July to 2 October 2024 (ref 7) and the pattern returned in 2026 (ref 3).
notes.significance: The ministry raised its high-water-temperature disaster alert to 'Serious Level I' in 2026 (ref 3) and had set up an emergency response headquarters under its 2025 measures (ref 6).

records.title: Korea's coastal catch has fallen about 40% since the 1980s and squid landings to a tenth of their peak as seas warm
records.description: The Korean government reports that coastal fish catch fell from 1.51 million tonnes in the 1980s to about 910,000 tonnes over the past four years, and a National Institute of Fisheries Science study shows common squid catch dropping from a peak near 250,000 tonnes in 1996 to roughly 23,000 tonnes in 2023. Korean waters warmed 1.60 C from 1968 to 2025, more than double the global rise. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries is widening total allowable catch limits to 19 species from July 2026 and plans to cover all coastal and offshore fisheries by July 2030.

notes.harm: Coastal catch fell from 1.51 million tonnes in the 1980s to 910,000 tonnes over four years (ref 1) and squid catch from about 250,000 tonnes in 1996 to about 23,000 tonnes in 2023 (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The 2026 TAC plan puts anchovy, squid and hairtail under vessel-level allocations with sanctions for exceeding them (ref 3) and the fisheries plan decommissions low-productivity vessels (ref 4).
notes.scale: The figures are national coastal and offshore catches, a national coastline rather than a single stock (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The coastal decline spans four decades (ref 1), the squid decline since the mid-1990s with a sharp drop in 2015 (ref 2).
notes.significance: The ministry published the 2026-2027 TAC implementation plan covering 19 species and 623,079 tonnes (ref 3) and a five-year Basic Plan with a 4 million tonne output target (ref 4).

records.title: China's four-month summer fishing ban covers the Bohai, Yellow and East China Seas as stocks stay under pressure
records.description: China's agriculture ministry, public security ministry and coast guard ran a special enforcement operation from 1 May to 16 September 2025 under the annual summer fishing moratorium, which covers nearly 120,000 vessels in 11 coastal provinces. More than 4,000 vessels sailed for the East China Sea when it ended. Official figures cited by a Chinese think tank say the share of stocks within biologically sustainable levels fell from 90% in 1974 to 64.6% in 2019, and the 2024 campaign investigated 9,770 violations.

records.title: Court cancels Saemangeum airport plan beside the Getbol World Heritage tidal flats, but backers keep pushing
records.description: On 11 September 2025 the Seoul Administrative Court cancelled the basic plan for the Saemangeum International Airport, finding that the environmental assessment underestimated bird-strike risk and did not adequately assess effects on the Seocheon tidal flats about 7 km away. IUCN's 2025 outlook rates Getbol, Korean Tidal Flats 'good with some concerns', notes tidal flats fell about 65% since the 1950s and lists the airport among current threats. Birds Korea said in July 2026 that some decision-makers still insist on building it; the sources do not say whether the ruling was appealed.

records.title: Taiwanese white dolphin down to about 45-50 animals as Taichung Port expansion and offshore wind advance
records.description: A researcher at the National Museum of Marine Biology and Aquarium told a July 2025 press conference that only 45 to 50 Taiwanese white dolphins (Sousa chinensis taiwanensis) remain, down about 3% to 4% a year since monitoring began in 2002, with about 60% showing visible injuries. About 90% use waters near Taichung Port, where a 160-hectare reclamation for LNG tanks is planned. The IUCN Cetacean Specialist Group notes four offshore wind farms with 201 turbines operating on the west coast by end 2023 and calls for stricter noise rules.

records.title: MT Terranova fuel oil spill in Manila Bay: 41,849 fisheries claims collected and compensation under way
records.description: The Philippine tanker MT Terranova capsized and sank in Manila Bay on 25 July 2024 during Typhoon Gaemi while carrying 1,468,896 litres of intermediate fuel oil, polluting coasts in Bataan, Cavite and Manila. About 97 percent of the cargo was recovered and the wreck was removed on 21 September 2025, but claims are expected to exceed the owner's liability limits so the 1992 IOPC Fund is likely to pay; payments to Bataan fishers began in 2026.

notes.scale: Impact was confined to the east side of Manila Bay and adjoining coasts, a single bay (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.duration: The spill began on 25 July 2024 and wreck removal ended on 21 September 2025, with claim assessment still running in March 2026 (ref 1).

records.title: Raja Ampat nickel mining: four permits revoked in June 2025 as sediment runoff clouds coastal waters
records.description: Indonesia revoked four nickel mining permits in Raja Ampat on 10 June 2025 after an Environment Ministry investigation found environmental violations, while PT Gag Nikel continues on Gag Island. A September 2025 report by Auriga Nusantara and Earth Insight documented sediment run-off turning waters murky brown and bleached coral near mining sites, and said post-mining rehabilitation is very poor. Nickel mining on the small islands of Raja Ampat in West Papua, inside the Coral Triangle, drew a government response in June 2025: four mining permits were revoked and the fifth operator, PT Gag Nikel, was allowed to continue under closer supervision. Officials and campaigners reported sediment runoff from the Manuran and Kawe island operations and large forest clearance, while the cited sources describe the risk to coral reefs as potential rather than a measured loss. In April 2026 campaigners said heavy machinery remained on the islands.

records.title: Supreme Court ruling opens Philippine municipal waters to commercial fishing
records.description: A Supreme Court First Division resolution, reported in December 2024, upheld a Malabon trial court decision in a petition by Mercidar Fishing Corp. that declared small fishers' preferential access to the 15-km municipal waters unconstitutional. The Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources and the Department of Agriculture asked the Court to reconsider in January 2025, and fisherfolk groups, local governments and Oceana filed petitions and interventions. Oceana projects that up to 90% of the municipal waters of 533 of 884 coastal towns could open to commercial fishing; this is an advocacy estimate.

records.title: Philippine Supreme Court strikes down commercial fishing vessel tracking order FAO 266
records.description: The Philippine Supreme Court upheld a lower-court ruling that voided Fisheries Administrative Order 266, which required commercial fishing vessels to carry tracking devices and report catches to curb illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. The decision, dated 21 January 2026 and announced on 3 August 2026, found the order failed the rational basis test; BFAR and the fisherfolk group Pangisda Pilipinas filed motions for reconsideration on 14 August 2026. Implementation had been suspended since February 2022, when 1,566 of 2,997 targeted vessels had received transceivers.

records.title: Indonesia's quota-based fishing policy delayed amid stock and monitoring concerns
records.description: Indonesia introduced a quota-based measured fishing policy (PIT) in March 2023, capping total catch at 80% of estimated stock across six zones covering 11 fisheries management areas, but the start date was pushed to 2025. Mongabay reported that estimated stocks fell to 12 million tonnes and the share of management areas rated fully exploited rose to 53%, while scientists and the Ombudsman criticised the lack of updated stock data and monitoring capacity. A March 2026 study at Banda Aceh found limited port infrastructure and low fisher awareness.

notes.duration: The policy dates from March 2023 and a March 2026 study still describes implementation challenges at Banda Aceh (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: Issued as a formal ministerial decree and Government Regulation 11 of 2023, with a decree of 29 November 2023 delaying the start to 2025 (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Indonesia's mangrove restoration target slips to 2029 after a million hectares lost
records.description: Indonesia holds 3.44 million hectares of mangrove (2024 National Mangrove Map), about 20% of the global total, but has lost more than 1 million hectares over four decades. The Environment Ministry now targets rehabilitating 600,000 ha by 2029 under its enhanced NDC and identified 769,824 ha for rehabilitation, after the original 2024 goal was missed with about 150,000 ha restored by December 2024 according to the restoration agency. records.title: Indonesian shrimp farming hit by Cs-137 import alerts and US tariffs
records.description: US authorities detected radioactive caesium-137 in containers from Indonesia in August 2025, and FDA testing confirmed it in one frozen shrimp sample, leading to Import Alerts 99-51 and 99-52 that by October 2025 affected shrimp from Java and Lampung. Exports fell 54% year on year in October 2025 and January to June 2026 shipments were 14% below the same period of 2025. US tariffs of up to 32%, later cut to 15%, and antibiotic-residue concerns add pressure on pond farmers.

records.title: Ice-ice disease and epiphytes cut seaweed farm productivity in North Sulawesi
records.description: A peer-reviewed study at Nain Island in North Sulawesi found that ice-ice disease in farmed Eucheuma denticulatum was linked to epiphyte biofilm and thallus wounds, with warm, low-salinity water raising susceptibility. records.title: Plastic pellets from the sunken MSC Elsa 3 wash ashore along Kerala beaches
records.description: After the container ship MSC Elsa 3 capsized and sank off Kerala on 24-25 May 2025, plastic nurdles from its cargo came ashore along the state coast. Kerala reported hundreds of tonnes collected from beaches and six cetacean carcasses found, and a fishing ban out to 20 nautical miles was imposed. The Kerala High Court later ordered the shipping line to deposit compensation.

notes.scale: Pellets polluted beaches along the Kerala coast and were reported toward the Gulf of Mannar and Sri Lanka, a national coastline rather than one bay (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Volunteers were still searching beaches in early July, six weeks after the sinking (ref 3), and compensation litigation continued into September 2025 (refs 3, 4).

records.title: MSC Elsa 3 wreck off Kerala holds fuel and hazardous cargo as Kerala presses a multi-billion-rupee claim

records.title: IMO committee warns attacks on shipping near Hormuz could cause large-scale marine pollution
records.description: Since late February 2026 attacks on commercial ships around the Strait of Hormuz have trapped dozens of large tankers in the Persian Gulf and raised the risk of major oil pollution. On 1 May 2026 the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee adopted a resolution warning of large-scale marine pollution in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea and asked the Secretary-General to monitor environmental effects. Slicks have been documented near Qeshm and Kharg, and no estimate of crude reaching the sea exists.

records.title: Karachi discharges about 425 million gallons a day of untreated sewage into the Arabian Sea
records.description: A Karachi Water and Sewerage Corporation study estimates the city generates about 460 million gallons of sewage a day and treats only about 35 million, sending roughly 425 million gallons a day to the sea. Industrial and domestic wastewater flows through the Lyari River, and WWF-Pakistan's technical adviser says marine biodiversity around the Lyari and Malir river mouths has largely disappeared. The S-III treatment programme, started in 2014, has slipped to a December 2027 deadline.

records.title: Seawater has submerged more than 124 revenue villages in the Indus delta, a Dawn study finds
records.description: A Dawn study published in May 2025 found that over the past decade more than 124 dehs across six coastal talukas of Thatta and Sujawal districts have been submerged by the sea, with the total inundated area put at 1.2 million acres. Reduced freshwater flow below Kotri is cited as the main driver, with families leaving for Karachi. Further Dawn reporting in June 2025 describes rising sea levels, mangrove loss and displaced fishermen. Dawn's May 2025 analysis of Sindh revenue data found more than 124 dehs (revenue villages) across six coastal talukas of Thatta and Sujawal districts have been submerged by seawater in the past decade, after freshwater flows below Kotri Barrage fell. AFP reported in August 2025 that flows into the delta are down about 80 per cent since the 1950s, salinity has risen about 70 per cent since 1990 and fish, shrimp and crab stocks have suffered. Sindh runs a mangrove restoration programme, but reports say clearing for land grabbing and housing continues elsewhere in the delta.

records.title: Mumbai starts a new coastal flood and sea-level vulnerability assessment as exposure grows
records.description: The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation began a fresh study in September 2026 of the city's vulnerability to coastal flooding and sea-level rise, its first update in about five years. An RMSI analysis reported by Business Today found about 998 buildings and 24 km of roads could be affected by 2050, rising to about 2,490 buildings and 126 km at high tide. Reclaimed low-lying areas flood when heavy rain coincides with high tide.

records.title: Arabian Sea oxygen minimum zone shows upper-ocean deoxygenation while its core regains oxygen
records.description: The Arabian Sea has the world's thickest and most intense oxygen minimum zone. Two 2025 conference abstracts using BGC-Argo floats report that oxygen in the core rose about threefold from 2013 to 2022 and the zone thickness fell 13%, while upper-ocean oxygen declined with stronger stratification. The findings are not yet confirmed by a peer-reviewed paper that was opened.

records.title: Desalination brine raises salinity in parts of the Persian Gulf, modelling studies find
records.description: The Persian Gulf hosts about half of the world's seawater desalination capacity, and most plants discharge brine back into the Gulf. A 2019 modelling study found brine raised mean Gulf salinity by only 0.43 g/kg but by about 4.3 g/kg in the southwestern Gulf near the Arabian coast, and a 2020 follow-up found basin salinity resilient to present discharge. A 2019 global study attributed over half of world brine output to Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait and Qatar, and an August 2026 analysis again flags hot, hypersaline effluent zones.

notes.scale: The modelled effect reaches a regional sea, with four Gulf countries producing over half of global brine (refs 1, 3).

notes.significance: The sources are research papers, a news report and an opinion analysis; no regulator notice or order was found (refs 1 to 4).

records.title: Severe coral bleaching at Lakshadweep's Kavaratti atoll in 2024 on top of a halving of live coral cover since 1998
records.description: ICAR-CMFRI researchers recorded severe bleaching of hard corals across Lakshadweep after marine heatwaves that began in October 2023, and a Lakshadweep Department of Science and Technology scientist put bleaching at Kavaratti atoll at 84.6 per cent in 2024, against 41.9 per cent in 2020. A peer-reviewed 24-year study published in July 2025 found live coral cover at 12 reef sites on Agatti, Kadmat and Kavaratti fell from about 37.2 per cent in 1998 to about 19.1 per cent in 2022, and that Lakshadweep has no formal reef management.

notes.livelihoods: CMFRI researchers warned that coastal livelihoods, tourism and fisheries are at risk if heat stress continues, but no closure or income loss is documented (ref 1).
notes.scale: Bleaching was recorded at several islands, and Agatti was affected less severely than Kavaratti, so the impact is archipelago-wide rather than one reef (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Bleaching is recurring: Kavaratti recorded 81% in 1998, 65% in 2010, 41.9% in 2020 and 84.6% in 2024, and heatwaves also struck in 2016 (refs 3, 4).
notes.significance: The 2024 figure comes from the Union Territory's own science department and the 2025 study is peer-reviewed, but no formal notice or order has been issued, so this scores the formal-assessment level (refs 3, 4).

records.title: Endangered Arabian Sea humpback whales of about 80 animals face gillnet entanglement and ship strikes off Oman
records.description: A peer-reviewed health assessment found about two thirds of photographed Arabian Sea humpbacks bore scars consistent with entanglement in fishing gear and six had injuries consistent with vessel strikes. In February 2025 Oman's Environment Authority opened an investigation into a dead humpback found at Al Jazer in Al Wusta, and a June 2026 satellite-tagging study counted just over 80 whales in the Endangered population. A UN migratory species report said a regional conservation plan had not yet been agreed and the Concerted Action should be extended.

records.title: Masirah Island's loggerhead nesting population down 79 per cent, with about 2,000 caught in fisheries each year
records.description: Researchers reported a 79 per cent decline in the loggerhead nesting population on Masirah Island, Oman, one of the largest loggerhead nesting grounds in the world, based on about 30 years of data. The Environment Society of Oman estimates around 2,000 loggerheads are caught annually in local fisheries, and the population is listed Critically Endangered in the Northwest Indian Ocean. Oman's Environment Authority began a five-year nesting and hatching study in May 2022 under an agreement with the US Fish and Wildlife Service.

records.title: Gwadar fishers report a collapse of local catches blamed on illegal deep-sea trawling in Balochistan's waters
records.description: A Dawn feature published in April 2025 reports that fishers in Gwadar, Balochistan, say illegal, unreported and unregulated deep-sea trawling, mostly by vessels from Sindh, is depleting the sea. Balochistan's Marine and Fisheries Department says the Mobula ray (karinj) is effectively extinct locally and sawfish have disappeared, and officials describe enforcement of the 12-nautical-mile trawler limit and the June to July breeding-season ban as difficult. Fishers also allege bycatch of turtles, dolphins and sharks and report intimidation, including a fatal incident on 28 May 2024.

location.detail: Balochistan's roughly 750 km Arabian Sea coastline, centred on Gwadar. Coordinates are those of Gwadar city.

notes.harm: Balochistan's Marine and Fisheries Department says the Mobula ray is effectively extinct locally (17 sightings in 2021-2022) and the sawfish has disappeared, with sharp declines in sardines, mackerel, pomfret and shrimp reported (ref 1).

records.title: Kerala's sardine catch collapses from 3.9 lakh tonnes in 2012 to 3,297 tonnes in 2021 and stays volatile
records.description: Onmanorama reported in June 2024 that Kerala's sardine landings fell from 3.92 lakh tonnes in 2012 to 3,297 tonnes in 2021, recovered to 1.38 lakh tonnes in 2023, and that sardine prices had risen from about Rs 100 to over Rs 400 per kg while fishers expected a very poor 2024. A CMFRI study in Current Science, reported in October 2025, linked swings in small-sardine abundance to monsoon rainfall and upwelling and recommended species-specific warnings and local fishing restrictions. Kerala's annual 52-day monsoon trawling ban is in force.

notes.harm: Sardine landings fell from 3.92 lakh tonnes in 2012 to 3,297 tonnes in 2021 before recovering to 1.38 lakh tonnes in 2023 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Sardine prices rose from about Rs 100 to over Rs 400 per kg and a traditional fishers' leader warned the shortage would severely affect livelihoods, while a 52-day trawling ban restricts mechanised boats each monsoon (ref 1).
notes.scale: The impact covers Kerala's coast, with 3,800 mechanised boats and about 34,000 other boats registered in the state (ref 1).
notes.duration: The swing runs from 2012 through 2024 and CMFRI's 2025 study describes recurring fluctuation (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: CMFRI minimum legal sizes (10 cm for sardine) are being breached by catches of 7-8 cm fish, and a Current Science study proposes formal localised restrictions, a formal advisory-level signal (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: Nearly one lakh traditional fisherfolk are in Kerala per ref 1, but the number affected is not reported.

records.title: Abu Dhabi aerial survey puts dugongs at over 3,500 and sea turtles at about 8,000 in 2024 under a net ban and protected areas
records.description: The Environment Agency Abu Dhabi completed an aerial survey of more than 8,000 square kilometres of marine habitat and reported an estimated 3,500 dugongs in 2024, with mother-calf pairs making up 20 per cent of sightings, and about 8,000 sea turtles, roughly 30 per cent more than in 2015. The agency credits a fishing-net ban in the emirate's waters, nesting-site protection and marine protected area management. Abu Dhabi is described as the second-largest dugong habitat after Australia.

notes.livelihoods: The agency cites a fishing-net ban in the emirate's waters as a conservation measure, a restriction on fishers (ref 1).
notes.scale: The 8,000 km2 survey covers the emirate's waters, which is one habitat zone of the Gulf (ref 1).
notes.duration: EAD has run these aerial assessments since 2004 and the findings reflect a multi-year management programme, but no sustained harm is reported (ref 1).
notes.significance: The numbers are an official agency announcement and the net ban is a regulatory measure, which is a formal notice (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No human population figure applies.

A professor quoted said climate change is pushing even these hardy species to their limits. A secondary report says the 2017 bleaching event destroyed 73 per cent of Abu Dhabi's coral cover and that Abu Dhabi launched a Coral Gardens programme in May 2025 to deploy 40,000 artificial reef modules by 2030.

records.title: Bombay duck (bombil) catches fall at Satpati-Dahanu from a record 40,065 tonnes in 1979 as boats and trawlers crowd the fishery
records.description: A People's Archive of Rural India report said the Satpati-Dahanu bombil catch peaked at 40,065 tonnes in 1979 and was recorded at 16,576 tonnes in 2018, while bombil boats at Satpati fell from 30 to 35 in the 1980s to 12 by mid-2019. A May 2025 Krishi Jagran article describes growing concern about overfishing, catching immature fish and habitat disruption in the Palghar to Valsad fishery. Fishers blame trawlers and purse seiners and industrial pollution.

records.title: Commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman disrupted by attacks since 28 February 2026
records.description: After US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026, commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman have been struck by projectiles and explosive-laden boats, and the IMO Secretary-General said in April that there was no safe transit anywhere in the strait. Lloyd's List Intelligence reported over 90 attacks on commercial ships by 30 September 2026 and a severe threat level, with weekly transits still far below normal. Mines were reported to have made the strait's traffic separation scheme unusable for evacuations.

records.layer_rationale: A security-driven closure of the world's key oil and gas shipping lane, handled through IMO and flag-state decisions rather than a pollution or habitat process.

notes.livelihoods: The IMO Secretary-General said on 24 April that there was no safe transit anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz, and Lloyd's List Intelligence said major container lines still avoid the area in late September (refs 4, 6).
notes.scale: Incidents were logged across the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf near Basra and UAE waters, and the Gulf of Oman north of Muscat, a regional sea rather than one site (refs 1, 5).
notes.duration: Attacks began on 28 February 2026 and Lloyd's List Intelligence still rated the threat severe with an attack on a Kuwaiti-managed tanker on 28 September, more than seven months on (refs 1, 6).
notes.significance: IMO convened its 36th extraordinary Council session in March and the Council met again in July, where the Secretary-General reported the evacuation of stranded vessels was paused because safety could not be assured (refs 3, 5).

records.title: Thousands of seafarers stranded in the Persian Gulf as IMO evacuation plan is paused
records.description: The IMO Secretary-General put about 20,000 seafarers on roughly 1,600 vessels inside the Persian Gulf in March and April 2026. An evacuation framework that began at the end of June moved 136 vessels and 2,900 seafarers by 8 July, then was suspended after ships were hit; about 6,000 seafarers were still reported trapped. The IMO said sea mines made the usual traffic separation scheme unusable.

records.title: Iran's transit permits and fees for the Strait of Hormuz dispute the law of transit passage
records.description: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority has defined a management area in the Strait of Hormuz and says ships need permits and must pay what Iran calls service fees, while Iran's parliament reviewed a toll bill. The IMO Secretary-General has called Iran's attempts to impose a toll unlawful, and the United States rejected any tolls. Legal commentators say transit passage under UNCLOS may not be suspended, while Iran, which signed but never ratified the convention, points to its own law and to special-regime straits.

notes.livelihoods: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority requires permits and cargo details before entry, and Iran said vessels linked to adversary states would stay barred (refs 1, 3, 4).
notes.scale: The permit and fee zone covers the Strait of Hormuz, an international strait carrying about 20% of global seaborne oil and gas trade (ref 3).
notes.duration: The toll bill was under review by 23 March 2026 and the dispute was still live in the 27 July Dawn analysis, about four months (refs 1, 4).
notes.significance: The IMO Secretary-General called the toll unlawful, and Marine Insight reported the US rejected tolls; no court or tribunal ruling was found (refs 2, 3).

notes.livelihoods: QatarEnergy declared force majeure on some long-term LNG contracts with customers in China, Italy, Belgium and South Korea (ref 2).
notes.scale: The strikes hit Ras Laffan and relate to a gas field shared by two countries, and the CEO put the loss at 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The CEO said the damaged LNG facilities will take three to five years to repair (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Qatar's foreign ministry and other Gulf countries condemned attacks on energy infrastructure as violating international law, and force majeure notices were issued, but no court or tribunal ruling was found (ref 2).

records.title: Offshore sand and lime-mud mining blocks off Kollam and Porbandar drew Kerala protests and the auction was annulled
records.description: India's first offshore mineral auction, launched on 28 November 2024, offered 13 blocks including three off Kollam, Kerala for construction sand and three near Porbandar, Gujarat for lime mud. Kerala fishers, the state assembly and opposition politicians opposed the Kollam blocks, citing fishing grounds and reefs; Reuters reported the auction was annulled in December 2025 after weak industry interest and that India did not plan to revive it. The Mines Ministry said the blocks were set outside active fishing zones, which a University of Kerala report disputed.

location.name: Kollam and Porbandar offshore mineral blocks
location.detail: Three construction-sand blocks off Kollam, Kerala, and three lime-mud blocks off Porbandar, Gujarat; the seven Great Nicobar blocks are in another sea and not covered here

records.layer_rationale: A seabed-resource licensing plan opposed over fishing grounds and process, now shelved.

notes.harm: Al Jazeera cited a University of Kerala report that the Kollam sites sit in active fishing zones and that mining could raise turbidity and damage rocky reefs holding three-quarters of the coast's 30 coral species, but no mining took place (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: No mining went ahead, so no fishery disruption is documented; Down To Earth recorded fishers' fears for Kollam, which accounts for nearly 20% of Kerala's fish production by value (ref 3).
notes.scale: Blocks lay off two coasts, Kerala and Gujarat, so the finding spans a national coastline rather than one site (ref 1).
notes.duration: The auction was launched in November 2024 and annulled in December 2025, with Reuters reporting in April 2026 that it would not be revived (refs 1, 5).
notes.significance: The Kerala Assembly passed a unanimous resolution on 4 March 2025 and the Earth Sciences Ministry replied to a parliamentary query in December 2025; the annulment was reported by Reuters from anonymous sources (refs 2, 4, 5).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Three Kollam blocks hold an estimated 302.42 million tonnes of construction sand; the auction was annulled in December 2025 (Al Jazeera, 9 April 2025; Reuters via Baird Maritime, 1 April 2026).

signals: Al Jazeera reported Kollam has about 3,500 trawlers and more than 500 motorised boats dependent on the grounds (ref 2).
Reuters said officials expected weak bidder response and that the work was not economically feasible for companies (ref 5).

trend.note: The auction was annulled in December 2025 and India reportedly does not plan to revive it, though different blocks may be tried (ref 5).

records.title: Vadhavan mega-port near Dahanu opposed by Palghar fishing villages despite environmental clearance
records.description: India's Rs 76,000-crore Vadhavan container port on a reclaimed site about 6.5 km off Palghar district, Maharashtra received environmental clearance in February 2024 and a foundation ceremony in August 2024. Fishing villages and the Vadhavan Bandar Virodhi Sangharsh Samiti argue it threatens livelihoods and Dahanu's eco-sensitive status, and thousands marched to the Palghar Collector's office on 19-20 January 2026. Reclamation would use about 200 million cubic metres of sand dredged off Daman.

location.name: Vadhavan port site, Dahanu, Palghar
location.detail: Dahanu taluka, Palghar district, Maharashtra, on India's west coast; sand borrow area about 50 km off Daman

records.layer_rationale: A major port and reclamation project contested by fishing communities and over coastal-zone rules.

notes.harm: Mongabay reported critics' concerns for ghol, coral and 98.3 acres of mangroves near the site and that the EIA was incomplete, but no loss has been measured yet (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: Mongabay counted 5,333 fishing families in six villages and 7,525 fishers in ten others, with villagers fearing displacement; no displacement has yet been documented (ref 2).
notes.scale: Works concentrate on one site off Dahanu, with a separate sand borrow area off Daman (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The port was first proposed in 1997, shelved after local opposition, and revived in 2015, with protests continuing through January 2026 (ref 4).
notes.significance: The Environment Ministry cleared the project on 16 February 2024 and the Bombay High Court upheld the Dahanu authority's order in April 2024, formal decisions that the opposition continues to contest (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Mongabay India reported the project area is 17,471 hectares, with 51,991 objections at the January 2024 public hearing (23 April 2024).

records.title: Vizhinjam port operations begin amid disputed coastal erosion and fishers' catch complaints
records.description: Vizhinjam International Seaport in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala began trial operations in July 2024 and had handled 3 lakh TEUs and 150 ships by February 2025. A state expert committee found no significant link between port construction and erosion north of Kovalam while urging seawall repairs; fishers and activists dispute this and say the reports were not shared. A 2024 field study reported fishers travelling about 15 km for a catch against 5-10 km before.

location.name: Vizhinjam port, Thiruvananthapuram
location.detail: South Kerala coast; erosion reported north of Kovalam headland at Valiathura, Cheriyathura and Poonthura

records.layer_rationale: A new transshipment port whose construction impacts on a eroding coast and fishing grounds are contested.

notes.harm: The Kudale committee found no significant link between the port and erosion but called for urgent seawall and groyne repairs, while a draft white paper acknowledged worsening erosion attributed to storms (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: A field study of about ten interviewees reported fishers travelling about 15 km for a catch compared with 5-10 km earlier, observations rather than measured data (ref 2).
notes.scale: The disputed erosion stretch runs from Valiathura to Shanghumugham near one port (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Construction began in 2015, protests peaked in late 2022, and the dispute was still open when operations began in 2024-2025 (refs 1, 2, 4).
notes.significance: A state expert committee was formed on 6 October 2022 and submitted a final report in March 2024, a formal review that the state has not published (refs 1, 4).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The port has handled 3 lakh TEUs and 150 ships since trial operations began in July 2024 (South First, 5 February 2025).

measures.note: Draft white paper as reported by Onmanorama, 16 January 2023 (ref 3).

signals: South First said the port is expected to handle 15% of India's container transshipment (ref 1).
Fishers told Current Conservation they fish farther out and fuel costs are high when catches are poor (ref 2).

trend.note: No erosion measurements after the port opened were found in the sources opened.

corrective_actions: The Kudale committee recommended repairs to seawalls and groynes and coastal protection between Kovalam and Shanghumugham (ref 1).
CMFRI and ICAR studies found no current decline in fish production due to construction but recommended continued monitoring (ref 1).

records.title: Iraqi court annulment of the Khor Abdullah navigation agreement with Kuwait leaves Gulf waterway rules in dispute
records.description: Iraq's Federal Supreme Court annulled in 2023 the 2012 Khor Abdullah navigation agreement with Kuwait, ruling that parliament needed a two-thirds majority to ratify it. Kuwait's Foreign Ministry formally protested in September 2023, and in July 2025 Iraq's president, prime minister and parliament speaker agreed that parliament should re-legislate it and withdraw their appeals. No later resolution was found in the sources opened.

location.name: Khor Abdullah waterway
location.detail: Waterway between Kuwait's Bubiyan and Warba islands and Iraq's al-Faw Peninsula, Iraq's only direct access to the Gulf

records.layer_rationale: A bilateral maritime boundary and navigation dispute resolved or not through courts and treaties.

notes.harm: The cited sources document a legal and diplomatic dispute and no physical or health harm (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The pages describe risks to Iraq's maritime rights, port access and oil-export route but no closure or restriction of the waterway (refs 2, 4).
notes.scale: The dispute concerns Iraq's only Gulf access and its undefined maritime zones, a national coastline (refs 2, 4).
notes.duration: The court ruling came in September 2023 and the issue was still open in the August 2025 New Arab analysis, about two years (refs 1, 4).
notes.significance: Iraq's Federal Supreme Court annulled the agreement and Kuwait's Foreign Ministry delivered a formal protest note to Iraq's ambassador in September 2023 (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Iraq's Federal Supreme Court ruled the 2013 ratification law unconstitutional for lacking a two-thirds parliamentary majority (Shafaq News, 16 September 2023).

measures.name: Ratification majority required
measures.note: A rule rather than a measured quantity (ref 1).

signals: The New Arab cited analysts warning that Iraqi delay could be read as tacit waiver of maritime rights and put Grand Faw Port infrastructure at risk (ref 4).

trend.note: No development after August 2025 was found in the pages opened.

records.public_contact: Iraqi Federal Supreme Court and Kuwait Ministry of Foreign Affairs published channels.
corrective_actions: Iraq's three presidencies agreed on 8 July 2025 to have parliament re-legislate the agreement and to withdraw their appeals (ref 3).
Kuwait confirmed a 17 July 2025 technical and legal committee meeting (ref 4).
